title: Basic Percentages
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Basic Percentages from First Principles

introduction.overview: Percentage means 'per hundred'. It is a way to express a number as a fraction of 100. Percentages are used everywhere: discounts, interest rates, tax, marks, growth rates. Converting between percentages, fractions, and decimals is the most fundamental arithmetic skill after basic operations.
introduction.placementRelevance: Percentage is one of the most frequently tested topics in placement aptitude. It forms the basis for Profit & Loss, Simple/Compound Interest, Data Interpretation, and successive percentage problems. Percentage-based questions are common in the quantitative section of company aptitude rounds.
introduction.realWorldContext: Interest rates, GST calculations, salary hikes, election results, inflation data — all are expressed in percentages. Engineers regularly compute percentage changes, error margins, and efficiency improvements.

learningObjectives: Convert between percentages, fractions, and decimals fluently
Calculate X% of Y and 'what percent is X of Y' type problems
Find percentage increase and decrease correctly
Solve 'base value' problems (given the percentage and result, find the original)

coreDefinitions: Percentage: A ratio expressed out of 100. 'X%' means X per 100, i.e., X/100.
Percentage of a number: X% of Y = (X/100) × Y.
Base Value: If A is X% more than B, then B = A × 100/(100+X). If A is X% less than B, then B = A × 100/(100−X).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Percentages convert unlike fractions into a common scale of 100, making comparison easy. 3/7 vs 5/11 is hard to compare directly, but 42.86% vs 45.45% is instant. The percentage change formula always divides by the ORIGINAL value (the base), not the new value — this is the most common conceptual error.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Imagine a rectangle divided into 100 equal boxes. '35%' means 35 of those boxes are shaded. When calculating '20% of 350', think: 10% of 350 = 35, so 20% = 70. This halving/doubling of 10% is the fastest mental shortcut.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: X% of Y
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Find a percentage of any number.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Percentage Change
importantRulesAndFormulas.variables: Old = original value, New = changed value
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Always divide by the ORIGINAL (old) value.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Key fraction-percentage equivalents
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Memorize these for instant conversion in MCQs.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Any problem involving fractions and percentages.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Finding base value
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If X% of B = A, then B = (A × 100) / X
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Reverse calculation to find the original number.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: 'A certain number's 30% is 45. Find the number.'

mainNarrative: The most important thing to remember about percentage change is that the denominator is ALWAYS the original (base) value. If a price increases from ₹200 to ₹250, the increase is (50/200)×100 = 25%, NOT (50/250)×100 = 20%. The base is the value BEFORE the change.

Mental shortcuts using 10% as the building block: To find 10% of any number, simply move the decimal point one place left. 10% of 470 = 47. From this, compute 5% (half of 10%), 20% (double 10%), 15% (10% + 5%), 30% (3 × 10%), etc.

For percentage increase followed by percentage decrease: if a quantity increases by X% and then decreases by X%, the net result is NOT zero. It is a net decrease of (X²/100)%. Example: 100 increased by 10% = 110; decreased by 10% = 99. Net change: −1%.
When the problem says 'A is 25% more than B', the base is B. So A = 1.25B, which means B = A/1.25 = 0.8A. Equivalently, B is 20% less than A. This relationship is NOT symmetric.

deepDiveAspects.title: The 10% Building Block Method
deepDiveAspects.content: This is the fastest mental arithmetic method for percentages. Find 10% first (move decimal left), then build the required percentage. 10% of 680 = 68. So 5% = 34, 15% = 102, 20% = 136, 25% = 170, 30% = 204. This avoids multiplication entirely.

deepDiveAspects.title: Percentage vs Percentage Points
deepDiveAspects.content: If interest rates go from 8% to 10%, the increase is 2 percentage POINTS but 25% in percentage terms ((10−8)/8 × 100 = 25%). Placement tests sometimes test this distinction.

solvedExamples.title: Finding a Percentage of a Number
solvedExamples.question: Find 15% of 360.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Direct application of the percentage formula. Shortcut: 10% of 360 = 36, 5% = 18, so 15% = 36 + 18 = 54.

solvedExamples.title: Percentage Change Calculation
solvedExamples.question: A mobile phone's price increased from ₹12,000 to ₹15,000. Find the percentage increase.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The base for percentage change is always the ORIGINAL value (₹12,000), not the new value.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Dividing by the new price (15,000) instead of the old price — this gives 20%, which is wrong.

solvedExamples.title: Finding the Original Price (Reverse Percentage)
solvedExamples.question: After a 20% discount, a shirt costs ₹640. What was the original price?
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: If discount is 20%, then SP = 80% of Original. So Original = SP × 100/80.

steps.title: Set up equation
steps.explanation: After 20% discount, 80% of original remains. So 80% of Original = 640.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A 20% discount means the customer pays 80% of the original. To reverse: divide by 0.80 (or multiply by 100/80).
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Adding 20% to 640 (= 768) — this is wrong because 20% of 800 ≠ 20% of 640.

shortcutMethods.title: Percentage Speed Techniques

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Calculate X × Y, then divide by 100 — involves large multiplication.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Use the 10% building block: find 10% first (move decimal left), then scale. 15% = 10% + 5%. 25% = ¼. 12.5% = ⅛. Avoids multiplication entirely.

rulesForApplication: 10% of any number = number ÷ 10 (move decimal point one left).
To find X% of Y, try computing Y% of X if easier (they're equal): 4% of 75 = 75% of 4 = 3.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the wrong base in percentage change
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Confusing 'percentage of what' — the denominator must be the ORIGINAL value.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always ask: 'percentage change FROM what?' The 'from' value is the denominator.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming X% increase followed by X% decrease gives 0% change
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The base changes after the first operation.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Net effect of +X% then −X% = −(X²/100)%. Always a net loss.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding 20% to find original after 20% discount
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Reversing a percentage isn't the same as adding it back.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: After X% discount, original = discounted price × 100/(100−X).

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If the answer should be 'X% of 450' and options are 45, 67.5, 81, 90 — compute 10% = 45 and 20% = 90 to narrow down instantly.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Percentage problems are quick wins — solve them first. Most can be done mentally with the 10% method.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Percentage forms the foundation of DI (Data Interpretation) which carries the highest weightage in TCS NQT and Infosys InfyTQ.

summaryBullets: X% of Y = (X × Y) / 100. Also equals Y% of X.
% change = [(New − Old) / Old] × 100. Base is ALWAYS the original.
10% trick: move decimal one place left. Build other percentages from 10%.
Reverse: if result is R after X% increase, original = R × 100/(100+X).

keyTakeaways: The base for percentage change is ALWAYS the original/old value.
The 10% building block method eliminates multiplication — master it.
+X% then −X% is ALWAYS a net loss of X²/100 percent.
selfCheckQuestions: What is 12.5% of 240? Use the fraction shortcut (12.5% = 1/8).
A shirt costs ₹800 after a 20% increase. What was the original price?
If A is 25% more than B, what percentage is B less than A?
